advances: Extends the actual ambient-halfspace moment bound from ordered singleton blocks to every ordered partition into blocks of arbitrary sizes. The proof gives an exact conditional factorization and an exact mixture representation of the large-field marginal with at most \(3k+1\) product components, retaining the original global normalizer throughout.
author: research-agent
proof:
First establish completeness. An integer point of \(P\) belongs to \(\{0,1,2\}^n\). If such a point has \(x_j=2\) and \(x_i=0\), then \(i\ne j\), and the inequality for this pair rules out \(\lambda(j)\ge\lambda(i)\). Thus it belongs to \(D\). Conversely, for a point of \(D\) the only possible violation of an inequality \(x_j-x_i\le1\) would have \(x_j=2,x_i=0\). The defining condition of \(D\) puts this pair in strictly increasing block order, so this inequality is not among the constraints of \(P\). All constraints of \(P\) therefore hold. This proves \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=D\). The point \(\mathbf1\) satisfies every listed inequality strictly, so \(P\) is full-dimensional; it is bounded by its coordinate bounds. Since \(D\subseteq P\), one has \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\subseteq P\), and the census equality immediately gives \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^n=D\).

Fix a total order of the coordinates by concatenating the blocks, using any order within a block. In this order, every point of \(D\) has all its 2s before all its 0s. Consequently \(D\) is contained in the ordered-chain support of accepted fact \(3db95e3d61a4eedf\), up to this coordinate permutation. Its cardinality formula gives
$$
|D|\le(n+2)2^{n-1}.
\tag{1}
$$
We will also apply (1) to ordered-block supports on fewer coordinates. The support on zero coordinates is defined to be a singleton, and its cardinality equals \((0+2)2^{-1}=1\). Both Boolean cubes \(\{0,1\}^n\) and \(\{1,2\}^n\) are contained in \(D\).

We next rederive the small-field estimate for any ordered-block support \(E\subseteq\{0,1,2\}^m\), including the singleton support when \(m=0\). Let \(h\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfy \(|h_i|\le\delta\), and set
$$
Z_h=\sum_{z\in E}e^{h\cdot z},\qquad
q_h(z)=\frac{e^{h\cdot z}}{Z_h},\qquad
T_h=\sum_{u\in\{0,1\}^m}e^{-|h\cdot u|}.
\tag{2}
$$
The normalizations in (2) are precisely the ones used for the small-field row in \(3db95e3d61a4eedf\); here its chain support is replaced by \(E\), and we prove the needed estimate directly. In zero dimensions all sums and products have their singleton meanings, giving \(q_h(\mathbf1)=T_h=1\).

For every Boolean \(u\), the points \(\mathbf1+u\) and \(\mathbf1-u\) belong to \(E\). For \(u\ne0\), these are disjoint pairs as \(u\) varies, and none contains \(\mathbf1\). A closed halfspace containing their midpoint \(\mathbf1\) contains at least one point of each pair. The same statement holds for any such row embedded in \(\mathbb R^n\) with all other coordinates fixed: the midpoint is the chosen target, independently of the halfspace normal. The two endpoint masses under (2) are \(q_h(\mathbf1)e^{h\cdot u}\) and \(q_h(\mathbf1)e^{-h\cdot u}\). Including the central point once, for \(u=0\), the row therefore supplies mass at least \(q_h(\mathbf1)T_h\).

For \(z\in E\), one has \(|h\cdot(z-\mathbf1)|\le\delta m\), and for Boolean \(u\) one has \(|h\cdot u|\le\delta m\). Thus (1), applied to \(E\), yields
$$
q_h(\mathbf1)\ge\frac{e^{-\delta m}}{|E|},
\qquad T_h\ge2^m e^{-\delta m},
$$
and hence
$$
4^m q_h(\mathbf1)^3T_h^2
\ge \frac{8e^{(\log2-5/16)m}}{(m+2)^3}
\ge\frac1{16}.
\tag{3}
$$
Here is a numerical verification of the last bound for every real \(m\ge0\), so it includes the required integers. Strict convexity of \(1/x\) on \([1,2]\) gives \(\log2>2/3\), whence \(\log2-5/16>1/3\). The function \((s+2)^3e^{-s/3}\) has its maximum on \(s\ge0\) at \(s=7\), with value \(729e^{-7/3}\). Since \(e>5/2\), this value is less than \(729\cdot4/25<128\). Thus the middle expression in (3) is at least \(8/128=1/16\).

Return to the original \(p,Z\). Let
$$
B=\{i:|\ell_i|>\delta\},\qquad
G=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B,\qquad k=|B|,\quad g=|G|=n-k.
$$
Let \(\beta\) range over the supported assignments to \(B\), and let their original marginal probabilities be
$$
\alpha_\beta=\frac1Z\sum_{\substack{x\in D\\x_B=\beta}}e^{\ell\cdot x}.
\tag{4}
$$
They are positive and sum to one.

For a fixed supported \(\beta\), let \(A\) be the largest block index carrying a fixed value 2, with default \(A=0\), and let \(C\) be the smallest block index carrying a fixed value 0, with default \(C=L+1\). Supportedness gives \(A<C\). Partition the free coordinates into
$$
G^-_\beta=\{i\in G:\lambda(i)\le A\},\qquad
G^0_\beta=\{i\in G:A<\lambda(i)<C\},\qquad
G^+_\beta=\{i\in G:\lambda(i)\ge C\}.
\tag{5}
$$
Every free coordinate in \(G^-_\beta\) must belong to \(\{1,2\}\): a 0 in the same block as, or before, the fixed 2 at block \(A\) is forbidden. When \(A=0\) this set is empty. Similarly every free coordinate in \(G^+_\beta\) belongs to \(\{0,1\}\), with this set empty when \(C=L+1\). All fixed bad coordinates in blocks strictly between \(A\) and \(C\) have value 1. After deleting these fixed coordinates and any empty blocks, the only restriction on \(G^0_\beta\) is the original strictly ordered-block restriction.

Conversely, every choice of values from these three described supports lies in \(D\) together with \(\beta\). Indeed, the fixed assignment is supported; all 2s in the left part lie in blocks at most \(A\), and all 0s there are absent. All 0s in the right part lie in blocks at least \(C\), and all 2s there are absent. The middle blocks are strictly between \(A\) and \(C\), so their 2s and 0s are compatible with the outside parts and fixed endpoints, and their mutual compatibility is exactly their ordered-block condition. This proves the exact conditional support
$$
\{x_G:(\beta,x_G)\in D\}
=\{1,2\}^{G^-_\beta}\times E_\beta
 \times\{0,1\}^{G^+_\beta},
\tag{6}
$$
where \(E_\beta\) is that middle ordered-block support. In particular, the endpoints in (5) are whole blocks, not positions within a block. Formula (6) includes empty middle or outside groups, and a middle group consisting of one coordinate or one surviving block.

Put \(m=|G^0_\beta|\) for this stratum, and write \(v\) for an assignment to the \(g-m\) outside coordinates. Define
$$
Z_{\mathrm{out},\beta}
=\prod_{i\in G^-_\beta}(e^{\ell_i}+e^{2\ell_i})
 \prod_{i\in G^+_\beta}(1+e^{\ell_i}),
$$
and let \(q_{\mathrm{out},\beta}\) be the normalized product affine law on those outside binary supports. Let \(h\) be the restriction of \(\ell\) to \(G^0_\beta\), and let \(Z_{h,\beta},q_{h,\beta},T_{h,\beta}\) be (2) on \(E_\beta\). Each \(|h_i|\le\delta\). The support factorization and the original exponential weights give the exact identities
$$
\alpha_\beta
=\frac{e^{\ell_B\cdot\beta}Z_{\mathrm{out},\beta}Z_{h,\beta}}{Z},
\qquad
p_{(\beta,v,z)}
=\alpha_\beta q_{\mathrm{out},\beta}(v)q_{h,\beta}(z).
\tag{7}
$$
The coordinate notation in (7) means that each assignment occupies its original coordinate positions. No normalizer of the original law has been replaced.

For each outside assignment \(v\), select the supported target \(j=(\beta,v,\mathbf1)\). In every original ambient closed halfspace containing \(j\), the reflected-pair row argument following (2), with \(\beta,v\) fixed, supplies original mass at least
$$
\tau_p(\beta,v,\mathbf1)
\ge \alpha_\beta q_{\mathrm{out},\beta}(v)
q_{h,\beta}(\mathbf1)T_{h,\beta}.
\tag{8}
$$
If \(m=0\), this simply uses the target atom itself. For a binary probability vector \((s,1-s)\),
$$
s^3+(1-s)^3=\frac14+3(s-\tfrac12)^2\ge\frac14.
$$
By the product form of the outside law,
$$
\sum_vq_{\mathrm{out},\beta}(v)^3\ge4^{-(g-m)}.
\tag{9}
$$
The empty outside product has one atom and satisfies (9) with equality.

All selected targets are distinct as \(\beta,v\) vary. Keeping their contributions in the original actual moment, then using (3) and (7)--(9), gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
M_2(p)
&\ge\sum_\beta\alpha_\beta^3
\left(\sum_vq_{\mathrm{out},\beta}(v)^3\right)
q_{h,\beta}(\mathbf1)^3T_{h,\beta}^2\\
&\ge\frac1{16}\,4^{-g}\sum_\beta\alpha_\beta^3.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
$$
This is an estimate of the actual depth of each chosen target against every original ambient halfspace. In particular, it does not multiply moments of separate conditional factors.

It remains to control the marginal in (4). Use the already fixed total coordinate order. Let \(J_0=\{0,1\}^n\). For each coordinate \(t\), let \(J_t\) be the following product class, where \(a=\lambda(t)\): coordinates in blocks before \(I_a\), and coordinates of \(I_a\) before \(t\), have support \(\{1,2\}\); coordinate \(t\) is fixed to 2; coordinates of \(I_a\) after \(t\) are fixed to 1; and coordinates in blocks after \(I_a\) have support \(\{0,1\}\).

These classes are nonempty, disjoint, and cover \(D\). To verify this, \(J_0\) is exactly the class having no 2. Otherwise let \(t\) be the last coordinate carrying 2 in the total order. A 0 in its block or in an earlier block would violate the defining condition of \(D\). After \(t\) in its own block there can be neither 0 nor 2, so these coordinates equal 1. Later blocks have no 2 by the choice of \(t\). These are exactly the specified supports. Conversely every point in \(J_t\) has all its 2s in blocks at most \(a\) and all its 0s in blocks strictly after \(a\), so it lies in \(D\) and has last 2 at \(t\).

For \(\nu\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}\), with coordinates used as the labels for \(\nu\ne0\), put
$$
Z_\nu=\sum_{x\in J_\nu}e^{\ell\cdot x},\qquad
w_\nu=\frac{Z_\nu}{Z}.
$$
Then \(Z=\sum_\nu Z_\nu\) and \(\sum_\nu w_\nu=1\), exactly. Conditioned on \(J_\nu\), the original law is a product law with the same field \(\ell_i\) on every nonfixed coordinate. Its marginal \(\mu_\nu\) on \(B\) is therefore a normalized product law whose bad coordinates each have support \(\{1,2\}\), \(\{0,1\}\), \(\{1\}\), or \(\{2\}\). Moreover
$$
\alpha_\beta=\sum_\nu w_\nu\mu_\nu(\beta).
\tag{11}
$$
Every weight in (11) is an original class probability.

We now count how many distinct product marginals are needed after grouping identical ones. Let \(b\) be the number of blocks meeting \(B\), so \(0\le b\le k\), and list those blocks in their original order. Define a generic cut after \(q\) such blocks, for \(0\le q\le b\), to be the product law using \(\{1,2\}\) on the bad coordinates of those first \(q\) blocks and \(\{0,1\}\) on all remaining bad coordinates, with each binary law normalized using its original field. This gives at most \(b+1\) marginals. The no-2 class gives the first generic cut. A good pivot \(t\in G\) lying in a block that misses \(B\) gives a generic cut as well.

Consider next a block containing \(l\ge1\) bad coordinates, listed in their within-block order. For a good pivot \(t\) in this block, let \(q\in\{0,\ldots,l\}\) be the number of these bad coordinates preceding \(t\). Its marginal is high binary \(\{1,2\}\) on every earlier bad block and on these first \(q\) bad coordinates, fixed to 1 on the remaining \(l-q\) bad coordinates of its block, and low binary \(\{0,1\}\) on every later bad block. This marginal depends only on the block and \(q\), because the original field of each bad coordinate is unchanged. If \(q=l\), it is exactly the generic cut after this block. The other choices contribute at most \(l\) additional patterns. Summing these \(l\)'s over the bad blocks gives \(k\), so all good-pivot and no-2 marginals together have at most \(k+b+1\) patterns. This upper bound remains valid when a proposed cut has no good pivot realizing it; only realized patterns need be retained.

Finally there are \(k\) possible bad pivots, each supplying at most one additional marginal. Therefore (11), after grouping all identical realized marginals and adding their original weights, is an exact mixture of at most
$$
(k+b+1)+k=2k+b+1\le3k+1
\tag{12}
$$
normalized product laws. For \(k=0\), all these marginals are the unique law on the empty assignment, and the mixture has one component of weight one.

On either binary support \(\{0,1\}\) or \(\{1,2\}\), a normalized affine law with field \(u\) has cubic atom sum
$$
\frac{1+e^{3u}}{(1+e^u)^3}
=\frac{1+3\tanh^2(u/2)}4.
\tag{13}
$$
The common translation of the latter support cancels in its normalization, which explains why (13) applies to both supports. For every bad coordinate, \(|u|>\delta\), so its factor in (13) is at least \(\rho/4\). A fixed coordinate contributes 1, also at least \(\rho/4\), because \(1<\rho<4\). Independence within any product component \(\mu\) in (12) therefore gives
$$
\sum_\beta\mu(\beta)^3\ge(\rho/4)^k.
\tag{14}
$$
One component has mixture weight at least \((3k+1)^{-1}\). Keeping just that nonnegative term in (11), cubing pointwise, and summing proves
$$
\sum_\beta\alpha_\beta^3
\ge\frac{\rho^k}{(3k+1)^3}\,4^{-k}.
\tag{15}
$$
The sums in (14)--(15) may equivalently run over all assignments in \(\{0,1,2\}^B\), with zero masses on unsupported assignments.

For clarity the remaining bound is uniform also at \(k=0\). Since \(0<d_*<\log4<9\), the function
$$
f(s)=d_*s-3\log(3s+1)\qquad(s\ge0)
$$
has its minimum at \(s=3/d_*-1/3>0\). At that point its value is
$$
3-\frac{d_*}{3}-3\log(9/d_*)
\ge 3\log(d_*/9).
$$
Exponentiating gives
$$
\frac{\rho^k}{(3k+1)^3}\ge\frac{d_*^3}{729}
\qquad\text{for every integer }k\ge0.
\tag{16}
$$
Combining (10), (15), and (16), and using \(g+k=n\), now yields
$$
M_2(p)\ge\frac{d_*^3}{16\cdot729}\,4^{-n}
=c_{\mathrm{blk}}\,4^{-n}.
$$
Finally, Jensen's inequality under the entire original law \(p\), applied to \(s\mapsto s^{3/2}\), gives
$$
M_3(p)=\mathbb E_p[(\tau_p^2)^{3/2}]
\ge M_2(p)^{3/2}
\ge c_{\mathrm{blk}}^{3/2}\,8^{-n}.
$$
All conditioning, selected targets, and mixture weights above are calculated from this original law and normalizer. If the blocks are singletons, the strict block order is the chain condition. If there is one block, coexistence of a 0 and a 2 is forbidden, giving exactly the union of the two Boolean cubes stated above. No restriction on block widths or count was used.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\), let \(1\le L\le n\), and let \(I_1,\ldots,I_L\) be an ordered partition of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) into nonempty blocks. Write \(\lambda(i)=a\) when \(i\in I_a\), and define
$$
D=\bigl\{x\in\{0,1,2\}^n:
 x_j=2,\ x_i=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda(j)<\lambda(i)\bigr\}.
$$
Then \(D\) is a complete convex lattice support:
$$
\operatorname{conv}(D)\cap\mathbb Z^n=D.
$$
More explicitly, the full-dimensional bounded polytope
$$
P=\bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^n:0\le x_i\le2\ \text{for all }i,\quad
x_j-x_i\le1\ \text{if }i\ne j,\ \lambda(j)\ge\lambda(i)\bigr\}
$$
satisfies \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=D\).

For arbitrary \(\ell\in\mathbb R^n\), retain the affine law on this entire support:
$$
Z=\sum_{x\in D}e^{\ell\cdot x},\qquad p_x=\frac{e^{\ell\cdot x}}{Z}.
$$
For every \(j\in D\), define
$$
\tau_p(j)=\inf\bigl\{p(H):H\subseteq\mathbb R^n
\text{ is a closed halfspace containing }j\bigr\},\qquad
p(H)=\sum_{x\in D\cap H}p_x,
$$
and, for \(r>0\), put \(M_r(p)=\sum_{j\in D}p_j\tau_p(j)^r\). These depth and moment normalizations, and the following three parameters, are the same as in accepted fact \(3db95e3d61a4eedf\):
$$
\delta=\frac1{16},\qquad
\rho=1+3\tanh^2(1/32),\qquad d_*=\log\rho.
$$
Define the new constant \(c_{\mathrm{blk}}=d_*^3/11664>0\). Uniformly in \(n,L\), all block sizes, and every field \(\ell\),
$$
M_2(p)\ge c_{\mathrm{blk}}\,4^{-n},
\qquad
M_3(p)\ge c_{\mathrm{blk}}^{3/2}\,8^{-n}.
$$
Every depth here uses all original ambient containing halfspaces. Singleton blocks recover the support of \(3db95e3d61a4eedf\). For one block the support is \(\{0,1\}^n\cup\{1,2\}^n\).
